rationale: B wins because it stress-tests the fragile premise instead of decorating it. Its first angle asks "whether the subscriptions flow through mobile in-app purchase at all," which is the caveat that decides whether the 10-versus-30 story survives an editor; A wanders into "Patreon, Twitch, and YouTube" comparisons and a headline claiming "Millions of Unpaid Gaming Community Managers" with no support. A has useful bones, but B carries the burden of proof like an adult in the room.
gaps_in_A: "Millions of Unpaid Gaming Community Managers Just Got a Business Model" invents scale and labor status. The update says server owners can charge fees; it does not say millions, unpaid, or community managers.

"Patreon, Twitch, and YouTube" comparisons are not in the supplied facts. The 10% versus 30% app-store contrast is grounded; the creator-platform comparison needs sourcing before it belongs in the angle.
"ongoing regulatory scrutiny of app store fees globally keeps this topic warm" imports an external peg without evidence. If that peg is real, cite it; if not, it's newsroom cosplay.
The fee angle misses the decisive proof question: whether mobile subscribers trigger Apple or Google in-app purchase rules. Without that, the 10-versus-30 comparison may be apples to paperwork.
gaps_in_B: "moderator-to-merchant conversion: unpaid volunteer community managers" imports an unsupported labor frame. It may be true for many servers, but the update only gives server owners and paid roles/content.

"The prevailing belief is that a 200-million-user base plus a cheap take rate is an obvious win" invents an opponent. B admits the inference, but a contrarian angle needs a real market claim to push against.

"Next step: newsjack-detector" is a questionable operational call. For a known launch with four viable shapes, the sharper next move is journalist-fit-check unless there is already a live app-store-fee story to attach to.

"Apple takes 30%" is probably defensible shorthand, but the supplied fact is the 30% app-store standard. A strict pitch should avoid naming Apple unless the billing path and app-store comparison are verified.
